newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Malaysian Pacific power increasing - secret report.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian Pacific power increasing - secret report.

text.p: Malaysian influence over South Pacific countries is increasing as its timber firms help prop up some regional rulers, while other states look to Kuala Lumpur to counter Australian dominance, a secret Australian government report warns.

The 93-page briefing for Treasurer Peter Costello said Malaysian logging interests helped Solomon Islands leader Solomon Mamaloni remain a political force and had also supported Papua New Guinea leaders.

Fiji had sought closer ties with Malaysia in a bid to counter Australia's dominance of the South Pacific, said the document prepared by treasury officials with the help of the foreign affairs department and security agencies.
It was drafted for Costello as a briefing for the summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in the tropical resort town of Cairns earlier this month.

Publication by Reuters of some details of the briefing -- which also outlined embarrassing personal habits of Costello's 15 guests -- has sparked a political and diplomatic row for Australia's Liberal-National government.
The paper says the Solomon Islands faced economic crisis, but Mamaloni was an obstacle to much-needed economic reforms.
It said his political power was shored up by the backing of un-named Malaysian logging companies.
"Mamaloni's... dealings with loggers and others enable him to continue to dominate Solomon Islands politics," it says.
The paper says the Solomons government is behind on payments to local banks and businesses and foreign creditors.
It warns logging revenues, which have propped up government finances, will dry up around 2005 because of exploitation.
The briefing also says Papua New Guinea's former prime minister, Sir Julius Chan -- ousted in last month's national election -- had benefited from dealings with Malaysian logging companies.
It warns PNG politicians' personal interests will hamper efforts to combat abuses in the forestry sector.
"The government continues to drag its feet on reforming large scale abuses in sectors such as forestry because of politicians' personal interests," the briefing says.

Papua New Guinea's parliament is due to choose a new premier on Tuesday and Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Chris Haiveta -- who the report says was involved in Chan's logging dealings -- is a strong contender.

Australia and New Zealand are the forum's biggest economies, dwarfing the poorer island nations -- the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.
Australian aid is vital to the prosperity of many of these countries and Canberra also controlled some of the island nations before their independence.
Canberra has gone into damage control over the briefing's publication, which has sparked angry criticism from regional governments and calls for an apology from the Labor opposition.
Foreign Minister Alexander Downer ordered heads of mission in the South Pacific to tell their host governments the document does not represent the government's views.
Nauru and the Cook Islands have condemned the briefing as offensive and wrong and Australia's Labor opposition attacked it as patronising and contemptuous.
Australian Workplace Relations Minister Peter Reith, one of the coalition's most senior officials, said on Sunday the document did not represent the government's views.
